claim: Behavioral responses to many odorants are not fixed but are flexible, varying based on organismal needs.
source: Behavioral responses to many odorants are not fixed but are flexible, varying based on organismal needs.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: Serotonin can increase or decrease appetitive behavior in an odor-specific manner in locusts.
source: Our results indicated that serotonin can increase or decrease appetitive behavior in an odor-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing differential POR responses to different odorants after serotonin injection.

claim: Serotonergic modulation enhanced odor-evoked response strength in the antennal lobe.
source: On the other hand, in the antennal lobe, serotonergic modulation enhanced odor-evoked response strength but left the temporal features or the combinatorial response profiles unperturbed.
evidence: This is supported by intracellular recordings from projection neurons showing increased spiking activity after serotonin application.

claim: Serotonergic modulation left temporal features of odor-evoked responses unperturbed.
source: On the other hand, in the antennal lobe, serotonergic modulation enhanced odor-evoked response strength but left the temporal features or the combinatorial response profiles unperturbed.
evidence: This is supported by analysis showing that ON and OFF response timing was maintained after serotonin application.

claim: Serotonergic modulation left combinatorial response profiles unperturbed.
source: On the other hand, in the antennal lobe, serotonergic modulation enhanced odor-evoked response strength but left the temporal features or the combinatorial response profiles unperturbed.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and PCA showing that ensemble activity patterns were preserved after serotonin application.

claim: Serotonin allows for sensitive and robust recognition of odorants.
source: This result suggests that serotonin allows for sensitive and robust recognition of odorants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that serotonin enhances response strength while maintaining odor identity information.

claim: A simple linear model with neural ensembles segregated based on behavioral relevance is sufficient to explain serotonin-mediated flexible mapping between neural and behavioral responses.
source: We show that a simple linear model with neural ensembles segregated based on behavioral relevance is sufficient to explain the serotonin-mediated flexible mapping between neural and behavioral responses.
evidence: This is supported by the linear regression model that successfully predicts behavioral outcomes from neural data.

claim: Appetitive odorants that are attractive while hungry may not drive the same behavioral response after feeding to satiety.
source: For example, appetitive odorants that are attractive while hungry may not drive the same behavioral response after feeding to satiety (Vogt et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Different neuromodulators are hypothesized to be involved in mediating state-dependent changes in neural and behavioral responses.
source: It is hypothesized that different neuromodulators should be involved in mediating state-dependent changes in neural and behavioral responses (Lizbinski and Dacks, 2017; Sayin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Serotonin is a key neuromodulator in insects that is linked with the regulation of many behaviors, including feeding.
source: In insects, serotonin (5HT) is a key neuromodulator that is linked with the regulation of many behaviors, including feeding (Tierney, 2020), socialization (Ries et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2004; Anstey et al., 2009), aggression (Rillich and Stevenson, 2018; Dierick and Greenspan, 2007), and mating (Chen et al., 2022; Pooryasin and Fiala, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Elevated levels of serotonin have been shown to decrease the time spent feeding and the amount of consumed food in blowflies and flesh flies.
source: Elevated levels of serotonin have been shown to decrease the time spent feeding and the amount of consumed food in blowflies and flesh flies (Dacks et al., 2003; Long and Murdock, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Drosophila larvae and adults, inhibition of neural serotonin synthesis or global increase of serotonin levels increases or suppresses food intake, respectively.
source: In Drosophila larvae and adults, inhibition of neural serotonin synthesis or global increase of serotonin levels increases or suppresses food intake, respectively (Neckameyer, 2010; Eriksson et al., 2017; Majeed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A spike in serotonin levels in the locust brain is highly correlated with the solitary stage.
source: A spike in serotonin levels in the locust brain is highly correlated with the solitary stage (Guo et al., 2013), whereas high levels of serotonin in the locust thoracic ganglion are known to trigger the transformation of solitary animals into gregarious ones (Rogers et al., 2004; Anstey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High levels of serotonin in the locust thoracic ganglion are known to trigger the transformation of solitary animals into gregarious ones.
source: A spike in serotonin levels in the locust brain is highly correlated with the solitary stage (Guo et al., 2013), whereas high levels of serotonin in the locust thoracic ganglion are known to trigger the transformation of solitary animals into gregarious ones (Rogers et al., 2004; Anstey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Serotonin modulation has been linked with increased activity and aggression in crickets and flies.
source: Serotonin modulation has also been linked with increased activity and aggression in crickets and flies (Dierick and Greenspan, 2007, de Boer et al., 2016), as well as a reduction in courtship behaviors, like male wing extension toward females and mating in flies (Pooryasin and Fiala, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Serotonin is known to reduce olfactory sensory neuron output through presynaptic GABAergic inhibition in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, the serotonergic release is known to reduce olfactory sensory neuron output to the following circuit through presynaptic GABAergic inhibition (Gaudry, 2018; Petzold et al., 2009; Lv et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Exogenous serotonin is known to increase the odor-evoked responses of second-order neurons in the insect antennal lobe and vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: In contrast, exogenous serotonin is known to increase the odor-evoked responses of second-order neurons in the insect antennal lobe and vertebrate olfactory bulb (Gaudry, 2018; Brill et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The serotonin-mediated increase in odor-evoked responses has been reported to be odor-specific and hypothesized to enhance the sensitivity to odorants in a state-dependent manner.
source: The serotonin-mediated increase in odor-evoked responses has been reported to be odor-specific and hypothesized to enhance the sensitivity to odorants in a state-dependent manner (Dacks et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Starved locusts opened their maxillary palps when encountering certain food-related odorants.
source: In this assay, starved locusts opened their sensory appendages close to the mouth, called maxillary palps, when encountering certain food-related odorants (Simões et al., 2011; Saha et al., 2013b; Nizampatnam et al., 2018; Chandak and Raman, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work describing the behavioral assay.

claim: Hexanol is a green-leaf volatile.
source: Note that hexanol (green) is a green-leaf volatile (Bertrand et al., 2021), and benzaldehyde (blue) is a putative locust aggregation pheromone Torto et al., 1994.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Benzaldehyde is a putative locust aggregation pheromone.
source: Note that hexanol (green) is a green-leaf volatile (Bertrand et al., 2021), and benzaldehyde (blue) is a putative locust aggregation pheromone Torto et al., 1994.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Linalool is used in many pesticides.
source: Whereas linalool (red) is used in many pesticides (Beier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HEX evoked supra-median (0.62) PORs.
source: It is worth noting that HEX evoked supra-median (0.62) PORs, while BZA and LOOL have a response close to the median (0.4) POR level (mean POR = 0.43 across odorants and locusts).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: BZA and LOOL have a response close to the median (0.4) POR level.
source: It is worth noting that HEX evoked supra-median (0.62) PORs, while BZA and LOOL have a response close to the median (0.4) POR level (mean POR = 0.43 across odorants and locusts).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: AMN elicited sub-median (0.29) PORs across locusts.
source: In contrast, AMN elicited sub-median (0.29) PORs across locusts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: The probability of PORs changed after 5HT injection but only for a subset of odorants (HEX and BZA).
source: Notably, we found that the probability of PORs (Figure 1C) changed after 5HT injection but only for a subset of odorants (HEX and BZA).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data comparing PORs before and after serotonin injection.

claim: The PORs to LOOL decreased after 5HT injection.
source: Intriguingly, the PORs to LOOL decreased after 5HT injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data comparing PORs before and after serotonin injection.

claim: Injection of saline or merely repeating the same set of odorants after a 3-hr time window did not produce any significant change in the PORs.
source: Injection of saline or merely repeating the same set of odorants after a 3-hr time window (similar time frame as before and after 5HT injection) did not produce any significant change in the PORs (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 show PORs to paraffin oil before and after 5HT application).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments showing no change in PORs with saline injection or time passage alone.

claim: PORs to the odorants tended to increase as a function of odor intensity.
source: First, even without serotonin application, it can be noted that PORs to the odorants tended to increase as a function of odor intensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose-response behavioral data presented in Figure 2.

claim: There was a detectable decrease in PORs at the highest concentration of HEX and BZA.
source: However, note that there was a detectable decrease in PORs at the highest concentration of HEX and BZA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose-response behavioral data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Injection of serotonin increased the probability of generating POR for all concentrations of HEX and BZA.
source: Injection of serotonin increased the probability of generating POR for all concentrations of HEX and BZA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose-response behavioral data comparing responses before and after serotonin injection.

claim: Changes in PORs elicited by LOOL and AMN were only modestly modified after 5HT introduction.
source: In contrast, changes in PORs elicited by LOOL and AMN were only modestly modified after 5HT introduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose-response behavioral data comparing responses before and after serotonin injection.

claim: The reductions in behavioral responses at the highest intensity of HEX and BZA were no longer detectable or significant after 5HT treatment.
source: Furthermore, the reductions in behavioral responses at the highest intensity of HEX and BZA were no longer detectable or significant after 5HT treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose-response behavioral data comparing responses before and after serotonin injection.

claim: The baseline spontaneous firing patterns in individual projection neurons changed after bath application of serotonin.
source: Note that the baseline spontaneous firing patterns in individual projection neurons changed after bath application of serotonin.
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings comparing spontaneous activity before and after serotonin application.

claim: The PNs fired spontaneous bursts of spikes after serotonin exposure.
source: The PNs fired spontaneous bursts of spikes after serotonin exposure (Figure 3A [before 5HT] vs. Figure 3B [after 5HT]).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings and raster plots showing bursty firing after serotonin application.

claim: The ISI distributions after 5HT application showed a left shift, indicating that pairs of consecutive spikes occurred in quick succession.
source: The ISI distributions after 5HT application showed a left shift, indicating that pairs of consecutive spikes occurred in quick succession (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of inter-spike interval distributions from intracellular recordings.

claim: The median values for the ISI distribution reduced significantly for each PN recorded after serotonin application.
source: Consistent with these results, the median values for the ISI distribution reduced significantly for each PN recorded (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of inter-spike interval data from intracellular recordings.

claim: Serotonin altered the excitability of PNs and induced bursts of spikes.
source: Clustering closer to the X-axis indicates that serotonin altered the excitability of PNs and induced bursts of spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of median ISI values before and after serotonin application.

claim: The total spiking activity in individual PNs monotonically increased with the magnitude of the current injection before serotonin application.
source: In addition, we found that the total spiking activity in individual PNs monotonically increased with the magnitude of the current injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by current injection experiments showing dose-response relationships.

claim: After serotonin injection, the spiking activity remained relatively stable and did not systematically vary with the magnitude of the current injection.
source: However, after serotonin injection we found that the spiking activity remained relatively stable and did not systematically vary with the magnitude of the current injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by current injection experiments comparing responses before and after serotonin application.

claim: There are changes in excitability at the level of individual PNs after serotonin application.
source: While the changes in odor-evoked responses may incorporate both excitability changes in individual PNs and recurrent feedback inhibition through GABAergic LNs, these results from our current injection experiments unambiguously indicate that there are changes in excitability at the level of individual PNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by current injection experiments showing altered input-output relationships after serotonin application.

claim: PNs responded to odorants by increasing their spiking activity either during odor presentation (ON response) or after stimulus termination (OFF response).
source: Consistent with previous observations, PNs responded to odorants by increasing their spiking activity either during odor presentation (ON response) or after stimulus termination (OFF response) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings showing different temporal response patterns.

claim: Odor-evoked response patterns were consistent across trials.
source: These odor-evoked response patterns were consistent across trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by raster plots showing reproducible responses across multiple trials.

claim: The stimulus-evoked ON and OFF responses remained intact after 5HT application.
source: As can be noted, the stimulus-evoked ON and OFF responses in these four representative PNs remained intact after 5HT application.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of response timing before and after serotonin application.

claim: For a majority of the PNs that exhibited either an ON or OFF response, the response timing was maintained after 5HT application.
source: We found that for a majority of the PNs in our dataset that exhibited either an ON or OFF response, the response timing was maintained after 5HT application (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic analysis of response timing across the dataset.

claim: ON responses tended to be more robustly maintained after the 5HT application compared to the OFF responses.
source: Notably, ON responses tended to be more robustly maintained after the 5HT application compared to the OFF responses (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of response consistency for ON vs OFF responses.

claim: Most of the nonresponsive PNs continued to remain inactive during the odorant presentation after serotonin introduction.
source: Furthermore, most of the nonresponsive PNs continued to remain inactive during the odorant presentation after serotonin introduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of response categorization before and after serotonin application.

claim: The total number of spikes evoked by an odorant increased after 5HT application during both ON and OFF time periods.
source: Our results indicate that the total number of spikes (i.e., response magnitude) evoked by an odorant increased after 5HT application during both ON and OFF time periods (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of spike counts before and after serotonin application.

claim: Mere introduction of saline or the solvent in which serotonin was diluted (HCl) did not alter the PN responses.
source: However, mere introduction of saline or the solvent in which serotonin was diluted (HCl) did not alter the PN responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments with saline and HCl.

claim: Serotonin modulates the excitability of individual PNs.
source: In sum, these results indicate that serotonin modulates the excitability of individual PNs, but only those PNs that were activated by an odorant tended to increase their response magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spontaneous and odor-evoked activity changes after serotonin application.

claim: Only those PNs that were activated by an odorant tended to increase their response magnitude after serotonin application.
source: In sum, these results indicate that serotonin modulates the excitability of individual PNs, but only those PNs that were activated by an odorant tended to increase their response magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis showing that nonresponsive neurons remained nonresponsive after serotonin application.

claim: The response timing (ON vs. OFF periods) was robustly maintained across PNs after serotonin application.
source: Further, the response timing (ON vs. OFF periods) was robustly maintained across PNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic analysis of response timing before and after serotonin application.

claim: Neural response trajectories during (ON) and after (OFF) odor presentation periods activated different subsets of PNs and therefore did not have much overlap during these time periods.
source: Neural response trajectories during (ON) and after (OFF) odor presentation periods activated different subsets of PNs and therefore did not have much overlap during these time periods.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA visualization of neural trajectories.

claim: The ON response trajectories before and after 5HT application overlapped with each other, indicating that the ensemble activity across the 82 PNs was similar before and after serotonin application.
source: Our results indicate that the ON response trajectories before and after 5HT application overlapped with each other, indicating that the ensemble activity across the 82 PNs was similar before and after serotonin application.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA visualization showing overlapping trajectories.

claim: The structure of spontaneous activity before and after serotonin changed, and as a result, the correlation between them became negative.
source: As can be noted, the structure of spontaneous activity before and after serotonin changed, and as a result, the correlation between them became negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of spontaneous activity patterns.

claim: The odor-evoked responses before and after 5HT application were highly correlated.
source: Consistent with the results from the PCA, we found that the odor-evoked responses before and after 5HT application were highly correlated.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative correlation analysis of high-dimensional response vectors.

claim: The identity of the odorant is robustly maintained by ensemble neural activity after serotonin application.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the identity of the odorant is robustly maintained by ensemble neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA and correlation analyses showing preserved ensemble response patterns.

claim: Both ON and OFF responses continue to preserve the information they carry about the odorant after serotonin application.
source: Both ON and OFF responses continue to preserve the information they carry about the odorant.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of temporal response patterns and ensemble activity.

claim: The linear regression model is equivalent to assigning a weight to each projection neuron and using the weighted sum of projection neuron responses to generate the observed POR output.
source: Note that this model is equivalent to assigning a weight to each projection neuron and using the weighted sum of projection neuron responses to generate the observed POR output.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical structure of the model.

claim: The antennal lobe projection neurons can be divided into two nonoverlapping ensembles: Encoding Ensemble 1 is assigned mostly positive weights and Encoding Ensemble 2 are assigned negative weights.
source: We hypothesized that the antennal lobe projection neurons can be divided into two nonoverlapping ensembles: Encoding Ensemble 1 is assigned mostly positive weights and Encoding Ensemble 2 are assigned negative weights (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the linear regression model.

claim: Odorants that evoke supra-median PORs should activate more neurons in Encoding Ensemble 1.
source: Odorants that evoke supra-median PORs should activate more neurons in Encoding Ensemble 1, and those that produce sub-median-level PORs are expected to activate neurons in Encoding Ensemble 2 more.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model architecture.

claim: The model architecture is similar to having 'neuron–anti-neuron' pairs where one decoding neuron weighs the positive contribution to generate PORs, and the second decoding neuron collects the negative contributions and suppresses the same behavioral output.
source: It is worth noting that this architecture is similar to having 'neuron–anti-neuron' pairs where one decoding neuron weighs the positive contribution to generate PORs, and the second decoding neuron collects the negative contributions and suppresses the same behavioral output.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model architecture in relation to known neural coding schemes.

claim: Such 'neuron–anti-neuron' pairs have been utilized for predicting overall motor outputs.
source: Such 'neuron–anti-neuron' pairs have been utilized for predicting overall motor outputs (Wu et al., 2022; Saha et al., 2017; Britten et al., 1992) and are highly consistent with the emerging view from other insect models that have shown mushroom body output neurons form segregated channels to drive opposing behaviors (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mushroom body output neurons form segregated channels to drive opposing behaviors in insects.
source: Such 'neuron–anti-neuron' pairs have been utilized for predicting overall motor outputs (Wu et al., 2022; Saha et al., 2017; Britten et al., 1992) and are highly consistent with the emerging view from other insect models that have shown mushroom body output neurons form segregated channels to drive opposing behaviors (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The simple linear regression-based model was sufficient to robustly predict the observed PORs.
source: Our results indicate that this simple linear regression-based model was sufficient to robustly predict the observed PORs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model performance shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HEX and LOOL activated highly distinct neural ensembles.
source: Furthermore, as expected, HEX and LOOL activated highly distinct neural ensembles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural response data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: HEX-activated projection neurons received mostly positive weights.
source: HEX-activated projection neurons received mostly positive weights and LOOL-activated neurons received negative weights (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the weight assignments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: LOOL-activated neurons received negative weights.
source: HEX-activated projection neurons received mostly positive weights and LOOL-activated neurons received negative weights (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the weight assignments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Any increase in positively weighted PN responses (HEX response after 5HT) should increase the overall POR.
source: Any increase in positively weighted PN responses (HEX response after 5HT) should increase the overall POR, whereas the increase in negatively weighted PN responses (LOOL after 5HT) should similarly decrease the behavioral output.
evidence: This is a prediction of the linear model based on the weight assignments.

claim: The increase in negatively weighted PN responses (LOOL after 5HT) should decrease the behavioral output.
source: Any increase in positively weighted PN responses (HEX response after 5HT) should increase the overall POR, whereas the increase in negatively weighted PN responses (LOOL after 5HT) should similarly decrease the behavioral output.
evidence: This is a prediction of the linear model based on the weight assignments.

claim: Segregating odor encoding into behavior-specific channels in the antennal lobe would allow serotonin to amplify neural responses to all odorants, while still generating odor-specific increases or decreases in behavior.
source: Segregating odor encoding into behavior-specific channels in the antennal lobe would allow serotonin to amplify neural responses to all odorants, while still generating odor-specific increases or decreases in behavior.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of how the model explains the observed data.

claim: Fed locusts responded less to HEX and BZA compared to hungry locusts.
source: Compared to the hungry locusts (Figure 1), the fed locusts responded less to HEX and BZA.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral data from fed and hungry locusts.

claim: The introduction of serotonin increased the appetitive PORs to HEX and BZA in fed locusts.
source: However, consistent with results from the hungry locusts, the introduction of serotonin increased the appetitive PORs to HEX and BZA.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from fed locusts before and after serotonin injection.

claim: The appetitive responses of fed locusts treated with 5HT were comparable or slightly higher than the responses of hungry locusts to the same set of odorants.
source: Intriguingly, the appetitive responses of fed locusts treated with 5HT were comparable or slightly higher than the responses of hungry locusts to the same set of odorants.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral data from fed locusts with 5HT and hungry locusts.

claim: Responses to LOOL and AMN reduced or remained unchanged in the fed locusts treated with 5HT.
source: It is worth noting that responses to LOOL and AMN, non-food-related odorants with weaker PORs, reduced or remained unchanged in the fed locusts treated with 5HT.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from fed locusts treated with serotonin.

claim: Serotonin influences food-driven behaviors in locusts.
source: Therefore, we conclude that, like in many species, serotonin influences food-driven behaviors in locusts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed effects of serotonin on appetitive responses in both fed and hungry locusts.

claim: Since 5HT increased behavioral responses in both fed and hungry locusts, the precise role of 5HT modulation and whether it underlies hunger-state-dependent modulation of appetitive behavior still remains to be determined.
source: However, since 5HT increased behavioral responses in both fed and hungry locusts, the precise role of 5HT modulation and whether it underlies hunger-state-dependent modulation of appetitive behavior still remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study in fully explaining hunger-state-dependent modulation.

claim: Prior results from a number of invertebrate and vertebrate models have shown similar changes in odor-evoked neural responses in the antennal lobe.
source: Prior results from a number of invertebrate and vertebrate models have shown similar changes in odor-evoked neural responses in the antennal lobe (Gaudry, 2018; Dacks et al., 2009; Kloppenburg and Hildebrand, 1995; Kloppenburg et al., 1999; Dacks et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The increase in the spiking activity of second-order neurons seems inconsistent with the serotonergic gating of sensory input through presynaptic inhibition.
source: The increase in the spiking activity of second-order neurons seems inconsistent with the serotonergic gating of sensory input through presynaptic inhibition (Petzold et al., 2009; Lv et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an observation about the apparent contradiction between different effects of serotonin.

claim: It is possible that the increased neural sensitivity could compensate for the decreased input from sensory neurons.
source: Hence, it is possible that the increased neural sensitivity could compensate for the decreased input from sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how serotonin can both reduce sensory input and increase PN responses.

claim: The change in input–output mapping as a result of serotonin introduction resulted in an increase in the behavioral response to different concentrations of HEX and BZA.
source: The change in input–output mapping as a result of serotonin introduction resulted in an increase in the behavioral response to different concentrations of HEX and BZA.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking neural changes to behavioral outcomes.

claim: Serotonergic modulation altered sensitivity to some odorants without altering the identity of the odorant.
source: Hence, serotonergic modulation altered sensitivity to some odorants without altering the identity of the odorant.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that response strength increased while ensemble patterns were preserved.

claim: These results are consistent with prior imaging studies in flies that reported odor-specific changes in glomerular activity.
source: These results are consistent with prior imaging studies in flies that reported odor-specific changes in glomerular activity (Dacks et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The segregation of neural responses based on behavioral relevance could happen at any neural circuit along the olfactory pathway.
source: It is worth noting that such segregation of neural responses could happen at any neural circuit along the olfactory pathway.
evidence: This is a general statement about where neural segregation could occur.

claim: Hexanol (high PORs) and linalool (low PORs) activate highly nonoverlapping sets of PNs in the antennal lobe.
source: Our extracellular recording data (Figure 6E) indicate that hexanol (high PORs) and linalool (low PORs) do indeed activate highly nonoverlapping sets of PNs in the antennal lobe.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neural response data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The segregation of neural activity based on behavioral relevance begins very early along the olfactory pathway.
source: Hence, our results suggest that the segregation of neural activity based on behavioral relevance begins very early along the olfactory pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that segregation is already present at the antennal lobe level.

claim: The modulation of feeding behavior by serotonin is widely conserved across invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: While serotonin is implicated in a range of behaviors, the modulation of feeding behavior is widely conserved across invertebrates and vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement about the conservation of serotonin's role in feeding behavior.

claim: The appetitive response evoked by hexanol was reduced in animals that were fed.
source: We found that the appetitive response evoked by a food-related odorant (HEX; green-leaf volatile; Bertrand et al., 2021) was reduced in animals that were fed.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing fed and hungry locusts.

claim: Serotonin application in locusts that were fed recovered back their appetitive response to HEX.
source: Notably, we found that serotonin application in locusts that were fed recovered back their appetitive response to HEX.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from fed locusts before and after serotonin injection.

claim: Serotonergic neurons could mediate a hunger-state-dependent switch in behavioral response preference (attraction vs. repulsion) to the same food-related odorant in fruit fly larvae.
source: Earlier studies have shown that serotonergic neurons could mediate a hunger-state-dependent switch in behavioral response preference (attraction vs. repulsion) to the same food-related odorant in fruit fly larvae (Vogt et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Adult Schistocerca americana of both sexes from a crowded colony were used for electrophysiology and behavioral experiments.
source: We used adult S. americana of both sexes from a crowded colony for our electrophysiology and behavioral experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

source: Briefly, all odorants were diluted to their 0.01–10% concentration by volume (v/v) in mineral oil.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Ammonium alone was diluted in distilled water.
source: Ammonium alone was diluted in distilled water.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

source: Therefore, we chose a very diverse odor panel that consisted of a food odorant (hexanol) (Bertrand et al., 2021), a sexual maturation pheromone (4-vinyl anisole) (Assad et al., 1997), and a putative aggregation pheromone (benzaldehyde) (Torto et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

source: Sixth-instar locusts of either sex were starved for 24–48 hr before the experiment or taken straight from the colony and fed blades of grass for the satiated condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

source: The odor pulse was 4 s in duration and the inter-pulse interval was set to 60 s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

source: After the initial set of POR experiments, a 0.1 M serotonin solution was injected directly into the locust's head.
